title: The Afternoon Brief: Pentagon in flux; Iran war escalates as U.S. strikes resume
dek: The Army secretary's resignation over officer removals leaves the Pentagon without civilian leadership as Iran retaliates for American strikes, oil prices climb, and courts block two Trump orders affecting elections.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: Thursday brought convergence of institutional strain at home and military escalation abroad: the Pentagon faces a leadership vacuum just as the Iran conflict enters a new cycle of strikes and counterstrikes, while federal judges blocked Trump administration actions on birthright citizenship and mail voting as the midterm election enters its final nine weeks.
bottom_line: The resignation of Army Secretary Driscoll amid Hegseth's officer purge, the resumption of U.S.-Iran strikes and Iranian retaliation, and federal blocks on birthright citizenship and mail ballot rules converge on Thursday to show parallel fault lines: Pentagon institutional stability, the Iran conflict's next escalation threshold, and whether election administration will survive legal and operational challenges in the nine weeks ahead. The honest read is that federal judges are now the primary brake on executive actions affecting voting, USPS faces untested systems weeks before ballots ship, and the Iran war shows no sign of breaking its strike-and-retaliation cycle. What to watch: whether Driscoll's replacement is announced and confirmed quickly; whether either the U.S. or Iran signals readiness to negotiate over Strait control or uses the next cycle to test escalation limits; whether Judge Talwani extends the mail ballot block before states begin shipping ballots; and whether USPS testing reveals the whistleblower's concerns are operative.
body: This morning's picture is one of simultaneous pressure on three fronts: Pentagon stability, the escalating Iran war, and the legal viability of administration election policies as voting begins.

The Pentagon crisis, which dominated the morning brief, has a midday update. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll's resignation Monday, accepted by Trump that evening, reflected weeks of tension over Defense Secretary Hegseth's removal of more than two dozen senior officers, according to desk reporting. A senior defense official told the desk that Driscoll had served as a buffer, pushing back through the White House on what the reporting describes as Hegseth's purge, though those efforts ultimately did little to slow it. Driscoll, an unconventional choice without national security experience, had arrived with a background in venture capital and Republican politics. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell is widely viewed as a potential replacement and has advocated for the job behind the scenes, according to officials familiar with the matter. The White House and Pentagon have offered strong public support for Hegseth; Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast defended his tenure as focused on capabilities, while Senate Armed Services Committee Ranking Member Jack Reed stated Hegseth was "unqualified" both operationally and temperamentally.

The military landscape Driscoll left behind is one of active operations. Concurrent with the leadership transition, the USS Abraham Lincoln arrived in Thailand on Wednesday after 286 days at sea supporting U.S.-Israeli operations against Iran. The ship made its first full port stop since deploying in November 2025, giving nearly 5,000 sailors and Marines their first shore leave in more than nine months. An investigation into reported attempted suicides aboard the vessel remains open.

The Iran conflict itself entered a new escalation cycle on September 2-3. The U.S. struck Iranian military targets along Iran's southern coast on September 2, killing at least 18 people according to Iran's health minister, including four civilians and two children at a wedding in Kuhestak. U.S. Central Command said the campaign targeted air defense sites, radar, and maritime assets, including two Iranian government tankers under a new tanker-for-tanker policy. Iran responded hours later by firing missiles and drones at U.S. bases in Jordan, Kuwait, and Bahrain; Kuwait and Jordan's night skies were illuminated by intercepted Iranian ordnance, according to desk reporting. President Trump said the campaign would not last long but threatened to hit Tehran "very hard" if the Strait of Hormuz conflict remains unresolved. Brent crude oil has climbed to around $95 per barrel since fighting resumed, up more than 30% from the war's start. Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the Crisis Group, cautioned that "at some point, one of the sides may see a need to escalate in order to break this cycle."

On the home front, the legal framework for the midterm election faces fresh challenge. U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman blocked Trump's August 6 executive order limiting birthright citizenship on September 2, issuing a 35-page ruling finding it "almost certainly unconstitutional" under the 14th Amendment and citing the Supreme Court's June 2026 ruling that blocked Trump's initial 2025 order. The August order focused on restricting birthright citizenship to certain groups, including those born to parents deemed alien enemies or working for foreign embassies. Boardman wrote: "This Court must, once again, preliminarily enjoin enforcement of the President's most recent attempt to strip the right to citizenship from them."

Judge Indira Talwani is separately deciding whether to extend a temporary restraining order on Trump administration mail ballot regulations with the midterm election 70 days away and states about to begin mailing ballots. Talwani imposed a 14-day temporary block on August 27; that order expires next week, and the judge has indicated she will rule as soon as possible on a longer-term extension through preliminary injunction. The administration has signaled it will appeal to the Supreme Court.

Democratic lawmakers are demanding the administration release $39.6 million in congressionally appropriated election security funds. Senators Alex Padilla and Rep. Joseph Morelle wrote that the money must reach states and local election offices, citing a March 2025 funding cut to the Election Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center. That center had provided free intelligence on hostile actors targeting election infrastructure; after cuts, it shifted to a paid membership model that "under-resourced communities" cannot afford. The lawmakers wrote that the Trump administration's removal of hundreds of CISA personnel compounds their concern, particularly given reported cyber and online election interference capabilities from Iran, Russia, China, and other state and non-state actors.

Meanwhile, a USPS whistleblower, represented by Whistleblower Aid's David Kligerman, alleges the Postal Service is deploying a new election mail system that has not been adequately tested and was completed in roughly eight weeks instead of one to two years. The whistleblower says the system has zero percent failure tolerance at each checkpoint and failed testing. The Postal Service is operating under a federal court order permitting continued work on the portal on a voluntary basis with states.

On the international side, President Trump told GB News he would not automatically support the UK in a potential Falkland Islands dispute, linking such support to UK and NATO naval contributions during the Iran war. Trump stated the UK "was not there to help" and that he "always reviews every position." The UK government responded that Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future" and that the UK's commitment to them is "unwavering." Argentine President Javier Milei is scheduled to make a televised statement on September 4 about what he describes as his nation's "historic" claim to the islands.

Other developments: Venezuela oil production expansion, DOJ reversal on immigrant reporting, ICE detention deaths, judicial proceedings in the Charlie Kirk shooting case, Markey's primary victory, Tiger Woods' reckless driving plea, flooding in Southeast Texas, Gloria Steinem's death, Supreme Court composition amendments, a Maltese businessman's acquittal, NBA penalties against the Clippers, Nepal-China flood toll, OpenAI litigation, Minneapolis shooting, Palestinian teenager deaths, and election system vulnerabilities.

What anchors today's thread is not chaos but institutional pressure points: the Pentagon without confirmed civilian leadership during war, courts intervening repeatedly in election administration weeks before voting starts, and the Iran conflict cycling through new escalation with no diplomatic off-ramp named. The calendar is moving faster than the legal remedies or leadership transitions can resolve.
